Hi Alice — thank you, and glad the demo was useful. I've summarized the answers below and looped in Ben and Marissa for technical and commercial confirmation. Short answers first, then examples.

TL;DR:
- System prompts are billed as input tokens.
- Tool outputs are billed as output tokens when produced by the model; if that output then becomes visible as input to a subsequent model call (e.g., you pass tool_result back into messages[]), it will also be billed as input on that subsequent call. We do not "dedupe" across calls.
- Billing is per-token with per-request rounding to the next whole token (no 4-token buckets). Streaming tokens are billed as they are emitted but still subject to per-request rounding on the final invoice line item.

Example (high level):
1) One chat request: system prompt = 40 tokens (counts input), user message = 60 tokens (input), model output = 180 tokens (output). Billed: input 100 tokens, output 180 tokens. Rounded per request (each request's input and output token counts are rounded up to nearest token).

2) Tool call example: if the model calls a tool and the tool returns 120 tokens which you include in the next model call as user/system context, you'll be billed 120 tokens as the tool's output on the first request + billed again as input tokens on the second request when the tool content is included in messages[].

3) Streaming: tokens emitted by the model are charged; we don't hold off charging until the stream completes for the purpose of metering, but the invoice groups charges per-request and applies rounding there.

We'll follow up with a detailed worked example and a short writeup you can share with procurement. Ben, can you add an exact numeric invoice example (matching the attachments Alice sent)? Marissa I may need a short paragraph suitable for the PO confirming this behavior.

Hi all — digging into the precise math, below is a concrete invoice-style example using Alice's sample payload (attached). I'm also calling out edge-cases we commonly see.

Assumptions (from sample_payload.json):
- Single user turn with a system prompt added server-side.
- Tool returns 120 tokens (plain text).
- Model produced 150 tokens on the initial call; next call included the tool output + a follow-up user message and produced 90 tokens.

Step-by-step billing (per request):
Request A (initial model call that triggered tool):
- input: system=35 + user=55 => 90 input tokens
- output: model produced 150 tokens before tool call; when model calls tool, the tool invocation itself is a request metadata event and not charged until tool output is emitted. If the tool is executed synchronously and returned 120 tokens, that 120 tokens is recorded as model output for billing on Request A (we tag them as "tool_output" in metering).
- Request A billed: input=90, output=150 + 120(tool) = 270 output tokens

Request B (follow-up model call including tool output in messages[]):
- input: tool_content=120 + user_followup=20 => 140 input tokens
- output: 90 tokens
- Request B billed: input=140, output=90

Invoice line items (we show unrounded then rounded; Redwood rounds each request's token counts up to the nearest whole token; since tokens are integer counts already, rounding is identity — note: fractional-token theory only applies for some internal heuristics, not public metering):
- Request A input billed: 90 tokens
- Request A output billed: 270 tokens
- Request B input billed: 140 tokens
- Request B output billed: 90 tokens
- Total billed tokens: input=230, output=360 => grand total tokens billed = 590 tokens

Edge cases / clarifications:
- "System" tokens: always counted as input. If you inject the same system text client-side across multiple users, each request is billed separately.
- "Tool" tokens are attributed to the request that produced them. If reused as input later, they are billed again as input. There is no automatic cross-request netting.
- Rounding: we do per-request rounding at token granularity (not at 4-token buckets). If a future rate card introduces micro-token pricing or sub-token fractionalization for internal optimization, we'll announce it; current public metering is integer tokens.
- Streaming: tokens emitted in-stream are attributed to the active request; metering records the streamed count. For long-lived streams we may show partial usage in near-real-time dashboards, and the invoice will reconcile per-request totals.

Hope this helps. Karthik — can you confirm this aligns with the audit logs format required by procurement (they sometimes ask for per-request JSON with token attributes)?
